description:
If Aliens Exist, Why Haven't You Met One?

Episode 43 of a daily journey through the universe. 👽
The Fermi paradox: hundreds of billions of stars in our galaxy, most with planets, billions of years for life to spread, and yet total silence. We look at Enrico Fermi's 1950 question, the Drake equation, and the possible answers.

segments.text: If aliens exist, why hasn't anyone ever met one? Scientists have a name for this puzzle.
In nineteen fifty, the physicist Enrico Fermi was having lunch with friends, talking about aliens. Suddenly he asked: but where is everybody?
segments.headline: Where is everybody?

segments.text: Here's why it's a good question. Our galaxy has hundreds of billions of stars.
And most of those stars have planets. Billions of them could be rocky worlds at the right distance for liquid water.
segments.headline: Billions of planets

segments.text: The galaxy is over ten billion years old. Even a slow civilization could have spread across it in a small fraction of that time.
So why don't we see anyone? No signals, no ships, no visitors. Just silence.
segments.headline: The great silence

segments.text: In nineteen sixty-one, Frank Drake wrote an equation to estimate how many civilizations might be out there. Depending on your guesses, the answer is zero, or millions.
segments.headline: The Drake equation

segments.text: Maybe life is common, but intelligence is rare. Maybe civilizations destroy themselves. Or maybe something stops nearly all life from getting very far. Scientists call that the Great Filter.
segments.headline: The Great Filter?

segments.text: Or maybe they are out there, and we've just started listening. We've searched only a tiny fraction of the sky.
segments.headline: Or we just started

segments.text: Either answer is mind-blowing. Either we are alone, or we are not.
Next stop: Interstellar Visitors. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for the next stop.
